passage: Saturday night. Spent the whole day making the perfect thesis schedule: eleven colours, a tab per chapter, deadlines in bold, even little icons for weekends. It looks amazing. Four hours went into it and I felt busy the whole time, almost proud. Parveen messaged asking how the writing was going, and I said “planning stage,” which is true. But when I opened the blank document to start the first paragraph, my stomach dropped and I closed it again and fixed a font colour instead. The sheet is beautiful and I have written nothing. I think the sheet is easier than the first sentence. — Tushar

qa.q: How many colours did Tushar use in the schedule?
qa.a: Tushar used eleven colours in the schedule.

qa.q: Why did Tushar's stomach drop when the blank document opened?
qa.a: Tushar is frightened of the first paragraph, and fixing the schedule feels safer than beginning the actual writing.

qa.q: What small step could Tushar take next instead of adjusting the sheet?
qa.a: Open the document and write one rough sentence or two for the first paragraph, and allow it to be bad.

qa.q: What might Parveen think on hearing “planning stage”?
qa.a: Parveen probably takes it as normal progress and does not know that Tushar has avoided the writing, so a kind follow-up question could help.

grounding: A student builds an elaborate schedule and feels progress while avoiding the frightening first step of writing.

passage:
Gurleen: how's the report going?
Asif: great!! made a tracker with 6 colours and a progress bar 😄
Gurleen: nice. how many pages written?
Asif: ...zero
Gurleen: 😅
Gurleen: that's a very pretty zero
Asif: ok but the tracker is really good
Gurleen: I believe you. what's the scary bit?
Asif: the first paragraph. what if it's bad
Gurleen: then it's bad and you fix it tomorrow. write one ugly line now, I'll wait
Asif: fine. 10 mins
Gurleen: go. no fixing colours during it
Asif: 😅 deal
(Twelve minutes later Asif sends a photo of a page with four lines on it.)

qa.q: How many colours does Asif's tracker have?
qa.a: Asif's tracker has six colours and a progress bar.

qa.q: What is Asif afraid of about the first paragraph?
qa.a: Asif fears the first paragraph will turn out bad, which is why the tracker felt more comfortable than writing.

qa.q: What worked in Gurleen's reply to Asif?
qa.a: Gurleen asked what the scary part was and asked for just one ugly line, which made starting small and safe for Asif.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel when the photo of four lines arrives?
qa.a: Gurleen is probably pleased and relieved that Asif started, and perhaps a little amused at the twelve minutes instead of ten. 😊

grounding: A student polishes a tracker to avoid the frightening first step of writing.

passage: Francis, I'll tell you about your aunt Lalremsiami, back when she was twenty and studying accounts in Aizawl. She had a final paper on company law. The night I visited her hostel, she showed me a schedule. Beautiful! Colours for each subject, little boxes for breaks, arrows everywhere. She had spent two days making it. "And how much law have you read?" I asked. She went quiet. None. The schedule felt like work, you see, but the real work frightened her. I told her, "Read one case tonight, just one." She did, grumbling. Next morning, she read two more. She kept that schedule, but stopped decorating it.

qa.q: How long had Lalremsiami spent making her schedule?
qa.a: She had spent two days making it.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami keep making the schedule instead of reading law?
qa.a: She felt afraid of the real work, and building the colourful schedule gave her a comforting sense of doing something.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Lalremsiami start studying?
qa.a: Agreeing to read just one case that night turned the frightening task into a small first step.

qa.q: How might Francis see his aunt after hearing this story?
qa.a: Francis might feel reassured that even his capable aunt struggled with starting and learned to stop hiding in planning.

grounding: An elder tells how a student built an elaborate schedule to avoid the frightening first step of real study.

passage: With the laptop charger broken and only forty percent battery left, Gautam had one evening to start his dissertation proposal, due in three days. He opened a spreadsheet instead. He colour-coded each day, added reading slots, gym, even laundry. His roommate Manoj looked over. "That's gorgeous. Written anything?" Gautam's jaw tightened. "I'm planning." The battery dropped to twenty percent. The proposal document still had just a title. Gautam felt a flash of panic. He closed the spreadsheet, opened the proposal and typed three messy sentences about his topic. The battery died at the fourth. But three sentences were more than yesterday.

qa.q: How much battery did Gautam's laptop have at the start?
qa.a: It had only forty percent battery left.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when Manoj asked if he had written anything?
qa.a: He felt defensive and uneasy, tightening his jaw, because the planning had been a way to avoid the frightening start.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Gautam used his limited battery on the colour-coded schedule; closing it and typing three messy sentences finally broke the avoidance.

qa.q: How might Manoj feel watching Gautam plan?
qa.a: Manoj seems amused but concerned, noticing that the beautiful schedule had not led to any written work.

grounding: Shows a student spending time on an elaborate schedule that feels productive while the actual first step stays untouched.

passage: Tanvir's desk in the Kolkata PG was covered in sticky notes of four colours. For three days he had been designing the perfect semester plan: coding in blue, lab reports in green, gym in yellow. Each evening he adjusted it and felt productive. His lab report on enzyme reactions, due Friday, was a blank page. On Wednesday, his friend Yamini dropped by. She glanced at the notes, then at the empty report. "This is very pretty avoidance," she said kindly. Tanvir laughed, then stopped. He was scared the report would be bad. He set a timer for twenty minutes and wrote the method section.

qa.q: What colour were Tanvir's lab report notes?
qa.a: His lab reports were in green.

qa.q: What was Tanvir really feeling while he kept adjusting the plan?
qa.a: He was scared that the report would be bad, and adjusting the plan let him feel productive without facing that fear.

qa.q: What small step helped Tanvir start the report?
qa.a: He set a timer for twenty minutes and wrote just the method section.

qa.q: How does Yamini see Tanvir's sticky-note plan?
qa.a: Yamini sees it as a way of avoiding the report, but she says so kindly, calling it pretty avoidance.

grounding: Illustrates a student making elaborate plans to feel progress while the frightening first step stays untouched.

passage:
"Yamini, you've been at that laptop since lunch. How's the essay?"
"Look, Sabina!" Yamini turned the screen. "A timeline. Research in green, outline in blue, drafts in purple. Every day till the deadline, in fifteen-minute slots."
"It's beautiful. How many words have you written?"
"Of the essay? Well… none yet. But the plan's ready."
"You said the plan was ready yesterday."
"Yesterday I didn't have the colours."
Sabina sat on the bed. "What's the first sentence going to be about?"
Yamini went quiet. "That's the problem. It's about why I want the scholarship. And every time I start, it sounds stupid."
"So the timeline is safer."
"…Maybe."
"Close the timeline. Write one bad sentence about why you want it. Just one. I'll wait."
Yamini opened a blank page. Her fingers hovered. She typed: "I want this because my mother never got to study." She stared at it.
"That's not stupid," Sabina said softly.

qa.q: How many words of the essay had Yamini written?
qa.a: None yet.

qa.q: Why did Yamini keep working on the timeline instead of the essay?
qa.a: Yamini was afraid the first sentence would sound stupid, so planning felt safer than starting.

qa.q: What did Sabina suggest, and why did it work?
qa.a: Sabina suggested closing the timeline and writing one bad sentence, which made the frightening first step small enough to take.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel reading Yamini's first sentence?
qa.a: Sabina felt moved and gentle, telling Yamini softly that it was not stupid.

grounding: Shows a student who builds a colour-coded plan to avoid the frightening first sentence of an essay, until a friend helps her start.
